title: Fourteen Days to Find Sh1.1 Billion: Keroche Takes On the Taxman
dek: In November 2006 the Kenya Revenue Authority reclassified Keroche's fortified wine and demanded back taxes within a fortnight; Tabitha Karanja went to court.

story.event: Challenging a backdated Sh1.1 billion tax demand in court, then losing the fortified-wine business to a tax change
story.summary: In a letter dated 29 November 2006 the Kenya Revenue Authority reclassified Keroche's fortified wines to a higher excise heading and demanded about Sh1.1 billion in back taxes within 14 days. Tabitha Karanja's company sought judicial review and on 6 July 2007 the High Court quashed the assessment as an abuse of power, but the 2007-08 tax changes priced fortified wine out of its market, and Keroche turned to ready-to-drink vodka and, in 2008, beer. The dispute returned after a 2017 Court of Appeal judgment and was still in the courts in 2020.
paragraphs: At the end of November 2006, a letter from the Kenya Revenue Authority reached Keroche Industries in Naivasha. Tabitha Karanja and her husband, Joseph, had been selling fortified wine since 1997: a cheap, hygienically made drink for low-income buyers who otherwise drank whatever their villages offered. Since then it had been taxed under tariff heading 22.04, at 45 per cent. The letter, dated 29 November, said that was a mistake. The wine belonged under heading 22.06, at 60 per cent, and the difference was owed back to 2002. With VAT and income taxes, the demand came to about Sh1.1 billion, payable within 14 days.

Fortified wine then brought in about 80 per cent of the company's revenue, Karanja later told Harvard Business School. One later account says the choice offered was to pay or face closure. Keroche had renewed its licence every year and paid duty on the old classification without objection. On 11 December it applied to the High Court for judicial review. Looking back in 2014 on a decade of such battles, Karanja said, "This is my country and I had to fight on."

On 6 July 2007 Justice Joseph Nyamu barred the authority from collecting, calling the demand an abuse of power: a tariff could not be changed years after a business had planned around it and then collected backwards. The ruling did not save the product. The 2007-08 tax changes moved fortified wine to the higher rate anyway, and the price put it beyond Keroche's customers. Karanja stopped making it. She later recalled asking, "what do we do for this same market?" Her answer was a ready-mixed vodka, Viena Ice. In February 2008 she borrowed Sh1 billion from Barclays, and in October Keroche launched Summit, its first lager.

The case did not end there. The authority appealed, and in 2017 the Court of Appeal ruled. Business Daily reported a win for Keroche that quashed the 2006 letter; the authority said the judgment went its way and set the 2007 decision aside. Both accounts agree the court allowed fresh assessments with proper notice, which were issued. In March 2020, more than thirteen years after the first letter, the High Court paused enforcement on condition that Keroche paid Sh500 million while it contested the bill.

quote.text: How often have I done myself a manifest injustice to avoid the hazard of having yet a worse done me by the judges, after an age of vexations, dirty and vile practices, more enemies to my nature than fire or the rack?
quote.locator: Book III, Chapter X, "Of Managing the Will"
quote.translator: Charles Cotton (1685), ed. W. C. Hazlitt
quote.source_title: Essays of Michel de Montaigne — Complete, tr. Charles Cotton, Project Gutenberg eBook #3600
quote.connection: Montaigne, a landowner who could absorb a loss, preferred swallowing small injustices to an age before the judges. Karanja, handed a fortnight to find Sh1.1 billion, chose the judges and was still before them thirteen years later. Neither choice was free.

reflection: Some fights cannot be refused, and Keroche's may have been one. Yet the case shows how a fight can be won on paper while the thing it was meant to protect slips away by another route. What carried the company on was not the judgment but Karanja's question about the same customers.

You may have your own long disputes: with a regulator, a supplier, an old disagreement at work. Now and then it helps to ask what the fight is for, and whether that thing can be looked after some other way while the argument runs its course. Some days the fight can wait while you tend to what it is for.
invitation: Name one dispute or grievance that is taking your energy. Write down what you are really trying to protect, and one small way to protect it today that does not depend on winning.

sources.title: Senator Tabitha Karanja (Creating Emerging Markets oral history, interviewed by Ramon Casadesus-Masanell, 2025)
sources.publisher: Baker Library Special Collections, Harvard Business School
sources.supports: Keroche founded in 1997 with her husband, starting with fortified wine; in 2007-08 a new excise tax made fortified wines unaffordable for customers; at the time 80 per cent of revenues came from fortified wine; Keroche dropped fortified wine and launched a ready-to-drink vodka; Summit Lager launched in October 2008.

sources.title: Relief for Keroche in ten-year legal war with taxman (Edwin Okoth, 19 March 2017)
sources.supports: KRA letter dated 29 November 2006 demanding Sh1.1 billion (Sh802.9 million income tax, excise and withholding tax, plus about Sh305 million VAT) after reclassifying the wine and backdating to 2002-2005; Justice Joseph Nyamu barred collection on 6 July 2007 citing abuse of powers; the Court of Appeal quashed the November 2006 letter, noted Keroche had renewed its licence annually since 1997 and paid duty under the old classification without objection, and kept its orders in force until KRA issued reasonable notices.

sources.title: KRA responds to Keroche on tax dispute history (press release, 26 March 2020)
sources.supports: KRA's account: reclassification from heading 22.04 to 22.06; assessments of Sh802,919,447 and Sh305,094,183; judicial review application No. 743 of 2006 filed on 11 December 2006; High Court judgment of 6 July 2007 quashing the assessments; Court of Appeal judgment of 3 February 2017 described by KRA as in its favour, directing reasonable notices; reissued assessments; on 16 March 2020 the High Court granted Keroche a stay on condition it paid Sh500 million.

sources.title: Keroche-KRA tussle: what it is and what it isn't (op-ed by the CEO of Keroche Breweries, 22 March 2020)
sources.supports: Keroche's account: Viena taxed under HS 22.04 at 45 per cent of ex-factory value until KRA disrupted the arrangement in November 2006, proposing HS 22.06 at 60 per cent and backdating; the High Court ruling of 6 July 2007; the 2007-08 Finance Bill then forcing the higher classification; KRA's appeal.

sources.title: Tabitha Karanja: The Keroche-KRA tussle: what it is and what it isn't
sources.supports: Republication of the same 2020 op-ed under Tabitha Karanja's name, identifying her as its author.

sources.title: How Kenya's beer queen succeeded against all odds (2 June 2014, first published by Good Governance Africa)
sources.publisher: How we made it in Africa
sources.supports: Naivasha; Joseph Karanja as her husband; in 2006 KRA ordered Keroche to pay within two weeks or face closure, and Karanja sued and won; 2006-07 budget doubled the tax on fortified wines, Keroche's mainstay; her quotation 'This is my country and I had to fight on'; KSh 1bn Barclays loan in February 2008; Summit lager launched in October 2008.

sources.title: Overcoming crisis after crisis: The story of Keroche Breweries (7 December 2015)
sources.publisher: How we made it in Africa
sources.supports: Karanja's account of the low-income market neglected and drinking whatever was available in villages, and of the hygienic, affordable fortified wine; the 2006 dispute: after a tariff change KRA demanded Ksh1.1bn within 14 days, and a judicial review concluded KRA was abusing its powers.

sources.title: Female beer boss who took on drinks giant (Jessica Ellis and Lillian Leposo, 12 March 2013)
sources.supports: Fortified wine business started in 1997; in 2007 taxes made it too expensive for her target customers, forcing her to stop producing fortified wine; her quotation 'what do we do for this same market?' and the move to ready-to-drink vodka; Summit launched in 2008.

sources.title: Tabitha's spirited fight in a brewing tax storm (30 July 2015)
sources.supports: Finance Minister Amos Kimunya's 2007 tax changes on fortified wines took Keroche's low-end products off the shelves and left it on the verge of closing; the ready-to-drink vodka later sold as Vienna Ice; Summit Lager launched in 2008.

sources.title: Landmark in Kenyan tax law (Paul Musyimi, 14 May 2008)
sources.supports: Contemporary summary of Keroche Industries Ltd v Kenya Revenue Authority & 5 others [2007] eKLR: licence classified under heading 22.04 from about 1997; letter of 29 November 2006 reclassifying to 22.06 (60 per cent against 45 per cent) and demanding about Kshs 1.1 billion within 14 days for 2002-2005; the court found retrospective application unreasonable, oppressive and an abuse of power and upheld the company's legitimate expectation.

cross_checks.claim: In a letter dated 29 November 2006 KRA reclassified Keroche's wine and demanded about Sh1.1 billion within 14 days.
The reclassification moved the wine from heading 22.04 (45 per cent) to 22.06 (60 per cent).
Keroche sought judicial review and on 6 July 2007 the High Court quashed the assessment.
The 2007 tax changes made fortified wine too expensive for Keroche's customers and it stopped making it, turning to ready-to-drink vodka.
Keroche launched Summit lager in October 2008.
The Court of Appeal ruled in 2017 and allowed KRA to issue fresh assessments with proper notice; the dispute was still in court in 2020.

research_notes: Amount: KRA's own figures (Sh802,919,447 plus Sh305,094,183), Business Daily (2017), the 2008 law blog and How we made it in Africa (2015) all give about Sh1.1 billion; Keroche's 2020 op-ed says Sh1.2 billion. The story uses about Sh1.1 billion. Backdating: How we made it in Africa says 'nine years', the 2020 op-ed 'five years', Business Daily and the law blog 2002-2005, and KRA 'income years 2002 to 2006'; the story says 'back to 2002'. Rate: the op-ed and the law blog say 45 per cent under 22.04; Business Daily (2017) says 40 per cent; the story uses 45. Date of the letter: Business Daily and the law blog give 29 November 2006 and the op-ed 'November 2006'; a Standard report found in search said October 2006, and How we made it in Africa (2014) says the dispute began with a 2003 accusation; the story uses the dated letter. Closure: only How we made it in Africa (2014) says the order was to pay within two weeks 'or face closure'; the story attributes it to 'one later account'. Founding: HBS and CNN say 1997; How we made it in Africa (2014) says the couple opened a small alcohol factory in 1992; the story says they had been selling fortified wine since 1997. Tax change: HBS says 2007-08 excise, CNN '2007', Business Daily (2015) Kimunya's 2007 changes, How we made it in Africa (2014) the 2006-07 budget, and the op-ed the 2007-08 Finance Bill; the story says 'the 2007-08 tax changes'. Court of Appeal: KRA says its 3 February 2017 judgment favoured KRA and set aside the 2007 decision; Business Daily (19 March 2017) reported it as a win for Keroche that quashed the 2006 letter; the op-ed says the court allowed an appeal to be heard when KRA produced supporting documents. The story gives both characterisations and the point they share. The Kenya Law judgment page ([2007] KEHC 3680) is behind a bot challenge and could not be read, so the 2007 holdings are taken from Business Daily, KRA and the 2008 law blog. The Star op-ed is signed only 'the CEO, Keroche Breweries'; People Daily published the same piece under Tabitha Karanja's name. The HBS transcript PDF is not publicly fetchable; only the interview summary page was used. Founder quotations: 'This is my country and I had to fight on' (How we made it in Africa, 2014, said of more than ten years of battles, not of 2006 alone, and framed that way); 'what do we do for this same market?' (CNN, 2013). The vodka brand is spelt Viena Ice in the Standard and Vienna Ice by HBS and Business Daily; the story uses Viena, the spelling of the wine brand in the court and tax documents. Arc set to setback rather than the slate's hard-responsibility: the court win was followed by the loss of the product line it was meant to protect. Wikipedia was not used.
